The comma is actually not allowed here. Heil, like Hail in English, is a command to greet or salute someone, not a way to address that person. For example, you would say "All hail the King" if you wanted everyone to salute the king. Just like if you were saying "Salute the King", there's no room for a comma there. "Salute, the King" is wrong. Here, the command "Heil Kleyno" similarly cannot have a comma.

I guess it really depends on how you read it then. You could read it as a generic command for everyone to Heil Kleyno. Or, and I still stand by this, it could be a person who is addressing Kleyno. Like "Hey, Steve!".

It's not the proper use for an ellipsis either. An Ellipsis is used when you're indicating omission, not when you want a pause.

I think different people have brains that work in different ways; you know how some people are more visual learners, other are better listening to an audio book, other have to do things hands-on ?

Personally when I read I tend to see the words as individual graphic elements with intrinsic meaning (like Chinese ideograms), and not as a way to transcribe phonemes. I don't really read with an inner voice. So if you substitute a word with an homophone, but with a different meaning, I will not read it (and pronounce it with the inner voice) the same and get its meaning from context: the written form has precedence and its out of place meaning is just confusing.

For example when I see the shape "their", I will not hear the sound [ðɛə(ɹ)] and then decide later the meaning: I just immediately process the concept of "belonging to, 3rd person". If I see "there", I get "place/location". So, as you say,

because my brain assumes what I'm about to read

and like when you listen to music, you expect some logical or harmonic progression. If indeed what I read after is coherent with what is expected, everything is good, and reading can be very fast. On the contrary if there is a false note or a non-sense word, there is an abrupt shock and stop and I have to re-read, slowly, and reconstruct the real meaning, probably from the sound of the words. It can be very irritating.
